categories.name: Web Browser Management and DNS Filtering

questions.text: Are important systems and data backed up daily to an offsite location with the ability to restore multiple versions back at least 30 days?
references: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CP-1, CP-2, CP-9, CP-10
NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems
CIS Control 11 - Data Recovery
Protecting Data from Ransomware and Other Data Loss Events: National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE), 2020
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 1, Asset Management Version 1.1
questions.why: Ransomware encrypts your live files and often any backups still connected to the network, so offsite copies with several days of versions are what let you recover without paying.
questions.fix: Set up automated daily backups to an offsite or cloud location that keeps at least 30 days of versions and stays disconnected (offline or immutable) from your network.

questions.text: Are data backups tested annually?
references: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CP-1, CP-2, CP-9, CP-10
NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems
CIS Control 11 - Data Recovery
Protecting Data from Ransomware and Other Data Loss Events: National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence (NCCoE), 2020
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 1, Asset Management Version 1.1
questions.why: A backup you have never restored may be corrupt or incomplete, and you find that out only during a ransomware crisis when it is too late to fix.
questions.fix: Schedule at least one full test restore each year to confirm the backups actually work and to learn how long a real recovery would take.

questions.text: Is malicious web content being blocked using DNS filtering via methods like DNS resolvers and DNS firewalls?
references: NIST SP 800-81-2, Secure Domain Name System (DNS) Deployment Guide
CIS Control 9 - Email and Web Browser Protections
Selecting a Protective DNS Service: National Security Agency, 2021
DNS protection – GCA Quad 9
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: SC-7, SC-20, SC-21, SC-22, AC-4
questions.why: A lot of ransomware reaches machines through malicious websites and links, and DNS filtering blocks those connections before the download can even start.
questions.fix: Turn on a protective DNS service (a filtering DNS resolver or DNS firewall) so requests to known-malicious domains are automatically blocked.

links.label: CIS Control 9: Email and Web Browser Protections

questions.text: Are web browser security settings managed?
references: Steps to Secure Web Browsing, National Security Agency 2018
CIS Control 9 - Email and Web Browser Protections
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: SC-7, SC-20, SC-21, SC-22, AC-4
Securing Your Web Browser, CISA: updated 2015
questions.why: Unmanaged browsers can silently run risky scripts, plugins, and downloads that quietly deliver ransomware onto a device.
questions.fix: Standardize and lock down browser security settings across the organization, disabling risky plugins and enforcing safe download and scripting policies.

links.label: CIS Control 9: Email and Web Browser Protections

questions.text: Are annual tabletop exercises that include phishing response scenarios conducted?
references: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: AT-2, AT-3, CP-4, IR-3
NIST SP 800-84, Guide to Test, Training, and Exercise Programs for IT Plans and Capabilities
NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 2, Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Nonfederal Systems and Organizations
questions.why: Phishing is a top way ransomware gets in, and practicing your response ahead of time keeps a real incident from turning into confusion and delay.
questions.fix: Run a yearly tabletop exercise that walks your team through responding to a phishing-driven intrusion, using a free CISA exercise package.

questions.text: Are users trained to recognize cyber threats like phishing?
references: NIST SP 800-177 Revision 1, Trustworthy Email
CISA and MS-ISAC Ransomware Guide
Cyber Readiness Institute’s Ransomware Playbook
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: AT-2, AT-3
questions.why: Employees who cannot spot a phishing email are the easiest entry point for ransomware, since a single click can compromise the whole network.
questions.fix: Provide regular security awareness training that teaches staff to recognize and report phishing emails, suspicious links, and unexpected attachments.

links.label: CIS Control 14: Security Awareness and Skills Training

questions.text: Is email filtered to protect against malicious content?
references: NIST SP 800-177 Revision 1, Trustworthy Email
CISA and MS-ISAC Ransomware Guide
Cyber Readiness Institute’s Ransomware Playbook
questions.why: Most ransomware arrives as a malicious attachment or link in email, so filtering that content stops many attacks before a user ever sees them.
questions.fix: Enable email filtering that scans for malicious attachments, links, and spoofed senders, and quarantines suspicious messages automatically.

links.label: CIS Control 9: Email and Web Browser Protections

questions.text: Is perimeter network traffic monitored?
references: NIST SP 800-137, Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) for Federal Information Systems and Organizations
CIS Control 13: Network Monitoring and Defense
CIS Control 12, Network Infrastructure Management
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: SI-4
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 2, Controls Management Version 1.1
questions.why: Ransomware crews probe and enter through your network edge, and watching perimeter traffic is how you catch the intrusion early.
questions.fix: Set up monitoring at your network boundary (firewall and IDS logs with alerts) and assign someone to review it for unusual inbound or outbound activity.

links.label: CIS Control 13: Network Monitoring and Defense
NIST SP 800-137: Information Security Continuous Monitoring

questions.text: Is internal network traffic monitored?
references: NIST SP 800-137, Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) for Federal Information Systems and Organizations
CIS Control 13: Network Monitoring and Defense
CIS Control 12, Network Infrastructure Management
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: SI-4
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 2, Controls Management Version 1.1
questions.why: Once inside, ransomware spreads sideways between machines, and only internal traffic monitoring reveals that movement before it reaches critical systems.
questions.fix: Monitor internal (east-west) network traffic so you can detect a device scanning or connecting to others in unusual ways.

links.label: CIS Control 13: Network Monitoring and Defense
NIST SP 800-137: Information Security Continuous Monitoring

questions.text: Are networks segmented to protect mission-critical assets?
references: NIST Special Publication 800-125B, Secure Virtual Network Configuration for Virtual Machine (VM) Protection
CIS Control 13: Network Monitoring and Defense
CIS Control 12, Network Infrastructure Management
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: SI-4
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 2, Controls Management Version 1.1
questions.why: A flat network lets ransomware jump from one infected machine to everything else, while segmentation confines it to a small area.
questions.fix: Divide the network into segments (VLANs or subnets) that isolate critical systems, and restrict traffic between them to only what is needed.

questions.text: Has the organization established a baseline of network traffic and is it used to identify anomalous activity?
references: CIS Control 13: Network Monitoring and Defense
CIS Control 12, Network Infrastructure Management
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: SI-4
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 2, Controls Management Version 1.1
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 4, Vulnerability Management Version 1.1
questions.why: Without knowing what normal traffic looks like, the sudden spikes and odd connections that signal a ransomware attack blend into the everyday noise.
questions.fix: Establish a baseline of normal network activity and configure alerts that flag meaningful deviations from it.

links.label: CIS Control 13: Network Monitoring and Defense
NIST SP 800-137: Information Security Continuous Monitoring

questions.text: Have the organization’s hardware and software assets been inventoried and is the inventory managed?
references: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CM-8
NIST SP 800-137, Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM)
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 1, Asset Management Version 1.1
CIS Control 1: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets
questions.why: You cannot protect, patch, or recover devices and software you do not know you have, and unknown assets are often where ransomware takes hold.
questions.fix: Build and maintain a current inventory of all hardware and software, updating it as assets are added or retired.

links.label: CIS Control 1: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets
CIS Control 2: Inventory and Control of Software Assets

questions.text: Has the organization removed all unsupported hardware and software from its operating environment?
references: CIS Version 7, Implementation Guide for Industrial Control Systems
CIS Control 1: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets
CIS Control 2: Inventory and Control of Software Assets
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: SA-22, PL-2, SA-3
questions.why: Outdated, unsupported systems no longer receive security fixes, leaving permanent holes that ransomware readily exploits.
questions.fix: Identify and remove or replace any hardware and software that is past end-of-life and no longer gets vendor security updates.

links.label: CIS Control 2: Inventory and Control of Software Assets

questions.text: Does the organization detect rogue hardware and alert key stakeholders?
references: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: IR-6
NIST SP 800-137, Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM)
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 1, Asset Management Version 1.1
CIS Control 1: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets
questions.why: Unauthorized devices plugged into your network can introduce ransomware or give an attacker a foothold that bypasses your defenses.
questions.fix: Use asset discovery or network access control to detect unknown devices and automatically alert your IT staff.

links.label: CIS Control 1: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets
NIST SP 800-137: Information Security Continuous Monitoring

questions.text: Does the organization quarantine and/or remove all rogue hardware?
references: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CM-8
NIST SP 800-137, Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM)
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 1, Asset Management Version 1.1
CIS Control 1: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets
questions.why: Detecting an unauthorized device does little good if it stays connected and can still spread ransomware or leak data.
questions.fix: Put a process in place to automatically quarantine or remove unknown devices from the network as soon as they are detected.

links.label: CIS Control 1: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets

questions.text: Are documented and approved secure configurations used to manage the organization’s hardware and software assets?
references: NIST SP 800-70 Rev. 4, National Checklist Program for IT Products
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CM-2, CM-3, CM-6, CM-8 (2), CM-9
NIST SP 800-128, Guide for Security-Focused Configuration Management
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 3, Configuration and Change Management Version 1.1
CIS Control 4: Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software
questions.why: Devices and software shipped with default or loose settings expose services and accounts that ransomware operators use to get in.
questions.fix: Adopt documented, approved secure configuration standards and apply them consistently to all hardware and software.

links.label: CIS Control 4: Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software

questions.text: Are standard baseline images used to control hardware and software configurations?
references: NIST SP 800-70 Rev. 4, National Checklist Program for IT Products
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CM-2, CM-3, CM-6, CM-8 (2), CM-9
NIST SP 800-128, Guide for Security-Focused Configuration Management
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 3, Configuration and Change Management Version 1.1
CIS Control 4: Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software
questions.why: Inconsistent, hand-built systems drift into insecure states that create openings for ransomware and slow down recovery.
questions.fix: Create standard hardened baseline images and use them to deploy and rebuild hardware and software consistently.

links.label: CIS Control 4: Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software

questions.text: Does the organization manage system configurations using security hardening guides?
references: NIST SP 800-70 Rev. 4, National Checklist Program for IT Products
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CM-6
NIST SP 800-128, Guide for Security-Focused Configuration Management
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 3, Configuration and Change Management Version 1.1
CIS Control 4: Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software
questions.why: Generic configurations leave optional features and weak defaults enabled that attackers exploit to plant ransomware.
questions.fix: Apply recognized security hardening guides (such as CIS Benchmarks) to lock down system configurations.

links.label: CIS Control 4: Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software

questions.text: Is all public-facing software patched for vulnerabilities within 15 days for vulnerabilities rated as “Critical” and 30 days for vulnerabilities rated as “High”?
references: CIS Control 7, Continuous Vulnerability Management
CISA Binding Operational Directive 19-02
CISA Security Tip (ST04-006) Understanding Patches and Software Updates
NIST National Vulnerability Database
NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 3, Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Technologies
questions.why: Internet-facing software with known flaws is one of the most common ways ransomware gangs break in, often within days of a vulnerability becoming public.
questions.fix: Patch public-facing systems on a strict schedule (Critical within 15 days, High within 30) and prioritize known-exploited vulnerabilities.

links.label: NIST SP 800-40: Guide to Enterprise Patch Management

questions.text: Are all internal-facing software and firewalls patched for vulnerabilities within 30 days for both vulnerabilities rated as “Critical” and for vulnerabilities rated as “High”?
references: CIS Control 7, Continuous Vulnerability Management
CISA Binding Operational Directive 19-02
CISA Security Tip (ST04-006) Understanding Patches and Software Updates
NIST National Vulnerability Database
NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 3, Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Technologies
questions.why: Unpatched internal systems and firewalls give ransomware room to spread and gain more control once an attacker is already inside.
questions.fix: Establish a patch process that closes Critical and High vulnerabilities on internal software and firewalls within 30 days.

links.label: NIST SP 800-40: Guide to Enterprise Patch Management

questions.text: Are all software and firewalls patched for vulnerabilities within 15 days for vulnerabilities rated as “Critical” and 30 days for vulnerabilities rated as “High”?
references: CIS Control 7, Continuous Vulnerability Management
CISA Binding Operational Directive 19-02
CISA Security Tip (ST04-006) Understanding Patches and Software Updates
NIST National Vulnerability Database
NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 3, Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Technologies
questions.why: Slow patching anywhere in the environment leaves exploitable gaps that ransomware actors actively scan for.
questions.fix: Tighten your patch program so all software and firewalls are fixed within 15 days for Critical and 30 days for High vulnerabilities.

links.label: NIST SP 800-40: Guide to Enterprise Patch Management

questions.text: Are all software and firewalls patched for vulnerabilities within 3 days for vulnerabilities rated as “Critical” and 7 days for vulnerabilities rated as “High”?
references: CIS Control 7, Continuous Vulnerability Management
CISA Binding Operational Directive 19-02
CISA Security Tip (ST04-006) Understanding Patches and Software Updates
NIST National Vulnerability Database
NIST SP 800-40 Rev. 3, Guide to Enterprise Patch Management Technologies
questions.why: Attackers often weaponize new vulnerabilities within days, so anything slower than rapid patching leaves a dangerous exposure window.
questions.fix: Mature your patch program to remediate Critical vulnerabilities within 3 days and High within 7 across all systems.

links.label: NIST SP 800-40: Guide to Enterprise Patch Management

questions.text: Are strong and unique passwords implemented throughout the entire organization?
references: NIST Applied Cybersecurity Division, Back to basics: Multi-factor authentication (MFA), 2021
CISA Creating and Managing Strong Passwords
Cyber Readiness Institute’s Cyber Readiness Program
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 1, Asset Management Version 1.1
Global Cyber Alliance Small Business Toolkit
questions.why: Weak or reused passwords are easily guessed or cracked, handing ransomware operators direct access to accounts and systems.
questions.fix: Require long, unique passwords for every account and provide a password manager so staff can realistically follow the rule.

questions.text: Is two-factor authentication implemented for all privileged (e.g. system administrators) and remote users?
references: NIST Applied Cybersecurity Division, Back to basics: Multi-factor authentication (MFA), 2021
NIST SP 1800-17, Cybersecurity Practice Guide: Multifactor Authentication for E-Commerce
NSA Transition to Multi Factor Authentication
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 1, Asset Management Version 1.1
Global Cyber Alliance Small Business Toolkit
questions.why: If an admin or remote-access password is stolen through phishing, multi-factor authentication is often the only thing that stops the attacker from using it.
questions.fix: Turn on two-factor authentication for all administrator and remote-access accounts first, since these are the highest-value targets.

questions.text: Is two-factor authentication implemented for all users?
references: NIST Applied Cybersecurity Division, Back to basics: Multi-factor authentication (MFA), 2021
NIST SP 1800-17, Cybersecurity Practice Guide: Multifactor Authentication for E-Commerce
NSA Transition to Multi Factor Authentication
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 1, Asset Management Version 1.1
Cyber Readiness Institute’s Ransomware Playbook
questions.why: Any account without MFA is a potential entry point, so extending it to everyone closes the gaps attackers look for.
questions.fix: Roll out two-factor authentication to all users, prioritizing phishing-resistant methods (such as security keys) where available.

questions.text: Is the principle of least privilege enforced through policies and procedures?
references: CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 1, Asset Management Version 1.1
National Security Administration, Least Privilege, IA Guidance Security Tips, 2017
National Security Administration, Top Ten Cybersecurity Mitigation Strategies, 2018
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CM-5
questions.why: When everyday accounts have more access than they need, one compromised user lets ransomware reach and encrypt far more of your data.
questions.fix: Write and enforce a least-privilege policy that grants each account only the access its role actually requires.

questions.text: Is least privilege enforced through technical (technology-based) restrictions?
references: CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 1, Asset Management Version 1.1
National Security Administration, Least Privilege, IA Guidance Security Tips, 2017
National Security Administration, Top Ten Cybersecurity Mitigation Strategies, 2018
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CM-5
questions.why: Policies alone are easy to ignore; without technical enforcement, over-privileged accounts still hand ransomware a wide path across systems.
questions.fix: Enforce least privilege with technical controls such as role-based permissions and removing local administrator rights, not policy alone.

questions.text: Are audit logs maintained for all privileged (e.g. system administrator) accounts?
references: NIST SP 800-92, Guide to Computer Security Log Management
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
CIS Controls Version 8
NIST SP 800-115, Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment
questions.why: Admin accounts are prime ransomware targets, and without logs of their activity you cannot detect misuse or reconstruct how an attack unfolded.
questions.fix: Enable and retain audit logs for all privileged accounts, and review them regularly for unusual actions.

links.label: NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management

questions.text: Is there a list of known bad software (a “Blocklist”), and is the software on that list being blocked?
references: NIST SP 800-167: Allowlisting
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CM-7(5)
CIS Controls Version 8
questions.why: Known malicious and unwanted programs are common ransomware delivery tools, and blocking them stops a recognized threat from ever running.
questions.fix: Maintain a blocklist of known-bad software and configure systems to prevent it from executing.

links.label: NIST SP 800-167: Guide to Application Whitelisting
CIS Control 2: Inventory and Control of Software Assets

questions.text: Has the organization documented a list of known approved software (an “Allowlist”)?
references: NIST SP 800-167: Allowlisting
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CM-7(5)
CIS Controls Version 8
questions.why: Blocking only known-bad software misses brand-new ransomware, while an approved-software list is a stronger foundation for stopping anything unexpected.
questions.fix: Document an allowlist of the software your organization actually needs and has approved for use.

links.label: NIST SP 800-167: Guide to Application Whitelisting
CIS Control 2: Inventory and Control of Software Assets

questions.text: Is the Allowlist organized by software publisher, and is that list used to allow only approved software to run on organizational systems?
references: NIST SP 800-167: Allowlisting
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CM-7(5)
CIS Controls Version 8
questions.why: An allowlist only protects you if it is actually enforced, so that unapproved or malicious programs simply cannot run.
questions.fix: Organize the allowlist by software publisher and enforce it so only approved applications are permitted to execute.

links.label: NIST SP 800-167: Guide to Application Whitelisting
CIS Control 2: Inventory and Control of Software Assets

questions.text: Has the organization developed an incident response plan?
references: CISA and MS-ISAC Ransomware Guide
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 5, Incident Management Version 1.1
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: IR-8
questions.why: Without a written plan, a ransomware attack becomes chaotic, and every delay in responding lets the damage and downtime grow.
questions.fix: Develop a written incident response plan that defines roles, steps, and contacts for handling a cyber incident.

links.label: NIST SP 800-61: Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

questions.text: Are cybersecurity incidents reported and escalated to the appropriate stakeholders?
references: CISA and MS-ISAC Ransomware Guide
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 5, Incident Management Version 1.1
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: IR-6
questions.why: If staff do not know how or when to report a suspected incident, ransomware can spread for hours before the right people even hear about it.
questions.fix: Define clear reporting and escalation paths so incidents reach the right internal and external stakeholders quickly.

links.label: NIST SP 800-61: Computer Security Incident Handling Guide

questions.text: Does the organization perform business impact assessments?
references: CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 6, Service Continuity Management Version 1.1
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 7, Risk Management Version 1.1
NIST SP 800-184, Guide for Cybersecurity Event Recovery
NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CP-2
questions.why: Without knowing which systems and data are most critical, you cannot prioritize protection or recovery when ransomware forces hard choices.
questions.fix: Perform a business impact assessment to identify critical systems, acceptable downtime, and recovery priorities.

links.label: NIST SP 800-184: Guide for Cybersecurity Event Recovery

questions.text: Has the organization defined organizational risk criteria and tolerances?
references: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: PM-9, RA-3
NIST SP 800-39 Managing Information Security Risk
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 7, Risk Management Version 1.1
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 6, Service Continuity Management Version 1.1
questions.why: Without defined risk tolerances, decisions about which ransomware risks to fix first become inconsistent and often too slow.
questions.fix: Define your organization's risk criteria and tolerances so security investment targets the risks that matter most.

links.label: NIST SP 800-39: Managing Information Security Risk

questions.text: Is role-based security training conducted?
references: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
CIS Controls Version 8
NIST SP 800-115, Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: AT-3, PM-13
questions.why: Different roles face different attack paths, and generic training leaves high-risk staff (admins, finance) unprepared for the tactics used against them.
questions.fix: Provide role-based security training tailored to the specific responsibilities and risks of each job function.

links.label: CIS Control 14: Security Awareness and Skills Training

questions.text: Is rogue hardware being detected?
references: CIS Controls Version 8
NIST SP 800-115, Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CM-8
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
questions.why: An unauthorized device on the network can carry ransomware or open a backdoor that skips your normal protections.
questions.fix: Deploy tools that detect unknown or unauthorized hardware connecting to your network.

links.label: CIS Control 1: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets
NIST SP 800-137: Information Security Continuous Monitoring

questions.text: Are users who attempt to install rogue hardware counseled against installing rogue hardware?
references: CIS Controls Version 8
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: AT-3
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
questions.why: Employees who plug in unauthorized devices, often unknowingly, create repeat openings for ransomware unless the behavior is addressed.
questions.fix: Counsel and educate users who attempt to install unauthorized hardware so the behavior is corrected.

links.label: CIS Control 14: Security Awareness and Skills Training
CIS Control 1: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets

questions.text: Has the organization documented a list of known approved software (an Allowlist) organized by software publisher and version number, and is that list used to allow only approved software to run on organizational systems?
references: NIST SP 800-167: Allowlisting
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CM-7(5)
CIS Controls Version 8
questions.why: Attackers can abuse outdated or tampered versions of otherwise trusted software, so allowlisting must be precise enough to catch them.
questions.fix: Extend the enforced allowlist to specify approved publishers and version numbers, allowing only those to run.

links.label: NIST SP 800-167: Guide to Application Whitelisting
CIS Control 2: Inventory and Control of Software Assets

questions.text: Have disaster recovery procedures been developed?
references: CISA and MS-ISAC Ransomware Guide
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 5, Incident Management Version 1.1
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: IR-1, CP-1, CP-2
questions.why: Ransomware can take whole systems offline, and without disaster recovery procedures, restoring operations can take far longer than the business can afford.
questions.fix: Develop disaster recovery procedures that document how to restore systems and data after a major disruption.

links.label: NIST SP 800-184: Guide for Cybersecurity Event Recovery

questions.text: Does the organization conduct annual incident response tabletop exercises that include ransomware response scenarios?
references: CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 5, Incident Management Version 1.1
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CP-4, IR-3
questions.why: Practicing a ransomware scenario in advance exposes gaps in your plan while it is safe to do so, not in the middle of a live attack.
questions.fix: Run a yearly incident response tabletop exercise built around a ransomware scenario, using a free CISA exercise package.

questions.text: Are incident response tabletop exercises performed at least twice a year?
references: CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 5, Incident Management Version 1.1
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CP-4, IR-3
questions.why: Response plans and staff change over time, so exercising only once a year can leave newer gaps untested when ransomware strikes.
questions.fix: Increase incident response tabletop exercises to at least twice a year to keep the plan and the team sharp.

questions.text: Is a physical incident response exercise performed at least once a year?
references: CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 5, Incident Management Version 1.1
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CP-4, IR-3, IR-4
questions.why: A tabletop discussion is not the same as actually executing recovery, and only a hands-on exercise shows whether your team can really restore systems.
questions.fix: Conduct at least one hands-on (functional) incident response exercise each year that actually tests your recovery steps.

questions.text: Are physical incident response exercises performed at least twice a year?
references: CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 5, Incident Management Version 1.1
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CP-4, IR-3, IR-4
questions.why: Recovery skills fade and environments change, so a single yearly hands-on exercise may not keep the team ready for a real ransomware event.
questions.fix: Perform hands-on incident response exercises at least twice a year to maintain recovery readiness.

questions.text: Has the organization implemented redundant systems where appropriate for the purpose of resiliency?
references: NIST SP 800-160, Volume 2, Developing Cyber Resilient Systems
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CP-2, CP-7, CP-6, CP-8, CP-9, CP-10, MA-6
questions.why: If ransomware disables a critical system with no backup in place, operations can halt entirely until it is rebuilt from scratch.
questions.fix: Add redundancy for your most critical systems so operations can continue if one is knocked offline.

links.label: NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 2: Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems

questions.text: Have redundant and resilient systems and data been implemented throughout the organization?
references: NIST SP 800-160, Volume 2, Developing Cyber Resilient Systems
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: CP-7, CP-8, CP-11, CP-13, PL-8, SA-14, SC-6, SI-17
questions.why: Isolated redundancy still leaves single points of failure that ransomware can hit, causing wider outages than expected.
questions.fix: Extend redundancy and resiliency across systems and data organization-wide so no single failure can stop operations.

links.label: NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 2: Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems

questions.text: Does the organization consider risk inheritance and exposure between its various interconnected systems?
references: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2, Risk Management Framework for Information Systems and Organizations
CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 7, Risk Management Version 1.1
CISA Security Tip (ST18-007): Questions Every CEO Should Ask About Cyber Risks
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: PM-9, CA-3
questions.why: Connected systems and vendors share risk, so a ransomware infection in one can spread into yours through trusted links you may have overlooked.
questions.fix: Map how your interconnected systems and third parties expose you to inherited risk, and address the weakest links.

questions.text: Does the organization apply quantitative risk analysis to remediation activities?
references: CRR Supplemental Resource Guide Volume 7, Risk Management Version 1.1
CISA Security Tip (ST18-007): Questions Every CEO Should Ask About Cyber Risks
NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: PM-9
questions.why: Without weighing the real cost and likelihood of each risk, remediation effort can go to minor issues while the gaps ransomware exploits stay open.
questions.fix: Apply quantitative risk analysis to prioritize remediation by potential impact and likelihood.

links.label: NIST SP 800-39: Managing Information Security Risk
